# 7. Guardrail metrics and stopping rules

The prior failures show why monetization must be managed as a retention and trust problem, not only a revenue problem.

## A. Core business metrics

Track by segment, platform, geography, acquisition source, and treatment:

- Revenue per MAU
- Revenue per retained user
- Paid conversion at 7, 30, 90, and 180 days
- ARPPU
- Trial-to-paid conversion
- Monthly recurring revenue
- Annual-plan mix
- Net revenue after refunds, app-store fees, and incentives
- Customer acquisition payback
- LTV/CAC
- Variable cost to serve
- Gross margin by tier

## B. Retention and engagement guardrails

Track:

- D1, D7, D30, D90 retention
- Weekly and monthly active users
- Session frequency and duration
- Completion of the core action
- Activation rate
- Repeat use of the value-generating feature
- Churn and cancellation rate
- Reactivation rate
- Uninstall rate
- Downgrade rate
- Time to first value

### Illustrative stopping thresholds

The exact thresholds should be calibrated to historical volatility, but a treatment should generally be paused for investigation if it causes:

- More than **1 percentage point** deterioration in D30 retention
- More than **0.5 percentage points** deterioration in D7 retention for a high-volume cohort
- More than **10% relative increase** in uninstall rate
- More than **15% relative increase** in cancellation within the first billing cycle
- More than **20% relative increase** in refunds
- Material deterioration in completion of the core action
- A statistically significant decline in organic referrals or reactivation

For a change involving a hard paywall or advertising, use stricter thresholds because the downside can compound quickly.

## C. Trust and product-quality guardrails

Monitor daily during launches:

- App-store rating
- One-star review rate
- Reviews mentioning ads, paywalls, price, or cancellation
- Support tickets per 1,000 users
- Payment failures
- Accidental purchase complaints
- Privacy or consent complaints
- Ad hide/report rates
- Latency and crash rates
- Feature-access confusion
- Cancellation friction

A rating decline of even a few tenths can materially affect organic acquisition. The team should compare rating trends against the control group and against seasonality, not rely only on aggregate rating.

## D. Segment-level protections

A positive aggregate result can conceal damage to an important segment. Require separate reporting for:

- New users
- Existing active users
- High-value users
- Users on older devices
- Users in lower-income regions
- Users acquired organically
- Users with accessibility needs
- Users with high support or cost-to-serve profiles

Keep a small holdout group for each major monetization strategy. This identifies:

- Whether revenue is incremental or merely accelerated

# Monetization Strategy: Increase Revenue Without Repeating the Paywall and Ad Mistakes

## 1. Strategic objective

The company should not attempt to monetize every user in the same way. The usage data already indicates that users receive materially different value from the product, so the strategy should be **segment-led and value-based**:

- Preserve a genuinely useful free product.
- Convert high-value and high-intent users to paid plans.
- Monetize low-intent users through carefully controlled advertising or partnerships.
- Charge heavy users for measurable incremental usage or premium outcomes.
- Avoid forcing users to pay before they have experienced the product’s core value.

The primary goal should be to increase **blended revenue per monthly active user**, not simply paid conversion.

A useful revenue equation is:

\[
\text{Revenue per MAU} =
(\text{paid conversion} \times \text{ARPPU})
+ \text{ad revenue per ad-supported user}
+ \text{partnership revenue per user}
\]

A plausible 12-month ambition, subject to category economics, might be:

- Increase paid conversion from under 2% to **4–6%**
- Increase paid-user ARPPU by **15–30%** through better tiering and add-ons
- Generate modest ad or partnership revenue from non-paying users without degrading retention
- Improve 90-day customer lifetime value while maintaining or improving app-store ratings

The company should not set a conversion target that encourages damaging paywall behavior. A lower conversion rate with materially higher retention and ARPU can be economically superior.

---

# 2. Segment users by value, intent, and cost to serve

The first step is to turn usage data into operational segments. The exact thresholds should be calibrated to the product, but the following structure is broadly applicable.

| Segment | Typical behavior | Value received | Likely monetization |
|---|---|---|---|
| Casual explorers | Low-frequency use, shallow sessions, limited feature breadth | Basic utility or entertainment | Free tier, light advertising, partnerships |
| Habitual free users | Frequent use of core features but little premium engagement | Repeated ongoing value | Free with limits, Plus subscription |
| High-intent individual users | Repeated use of premium-adjacent features, saves, exports, personalization, or advanced workflows | Clear personal productivity or outcome value | Plus or Pro subscription |
| Power users/prosumers | High usage volume, advanced feature use, willingness to pay for speed, quality, automation, or capacity | Significant recurring value | Pro subscription, usage-based add-ons |
| Team or business users | Shared workflows, collaboration, administrative needs, multiple users | Organizational value | Team/business plan, seats, usage bundles |
| Dormant or reactivatable users | Previously active, now infrequent or inactive | Uncertain or episodic value | Re-engagement offers, annual plan, partnerships; no aggressive monetization |

## Segment assignment should use behavior, not demographics alone

Relevant signals include:

- Frequency and recency of use
- Number of core actions completed
- Use of advanced features
- Consumption or creation volume
- Export, save, share, or collaboration behavior
- Device and platform
- Engagement with existing upgrade prompts
- Session depth and return frequency
- Cost to serve
- Whether use is personal, professional, or commercial
- Prior trial or subscription behavior

The segmentation model should be dynamic. A casual user who repeatedly reaches a valuable feature should move into a high-intent treatment, while a previously active user who has disengaged should not continue receiving aggressive upgrade prompts.

---

# 3. Recommended monetization mix

## A. Subscription tiers: the primary engine

Subscriptions should remain the central monetization model for users receiving recurring, differentiated value. The company should introduce a clear ladder rather than a single paid tier.

### 1. Free

The free tier should provide a complete core experience, not a crippled trial.

Retain:

- The primary use case
- Basic creation or consumption
- Core sharing or saving
- Enough usage frequency to build habit
- Access to the product’s principal “aha” moment

Limit or reserve:

- High-volume usage
- Advanced automation
- Premium quality or speed
- Deep personalization
- Large storage or history
- Collaboration and administration
- Export formats or commercial rights, where applicable
- Convenience features that save significant time

The free product must remain strong enough to support word of mouth and organic acquisition.

### 2. Plus or Personal

Designed for habitual users who want a better everyday experience.

Potential benefits:

- Higher usage allowance
- Ad-free experience
- Faster processing
- More history or storage
- Better customization
- Basic advanced features
- Cross-device continuity
- Priority support
- Limited premium credits

This tier should be priced as an accessible upgrade for users who have already demonstrated recurring value.

### 3. Pro or Power

Designed for high-intent users and prosumers.

Potential benefits:

- Substantially higher limits
- Advanced features and automation
- Premium output quality
- Batch processing
- Priority speed or capacity
- Advanced analytics
- Commercial-use rights
- Larger storage and export capabilities
- API or integrations, if appropriate

The Pro plan should not simply be “Plus with more units.” It should offer capabilities that produce a clearly superior outcome.

### 4. Team or Business

Introduced when usage data shows meaningful collaboration or commercial behavior.

Potential benefits:

- Shared workspaces
- Multiple seats
- Centralized billing
- Admin controls
- Usage visibility
- Security and compliance features
- Shared templates, assets, or history
- Support commitments
- Volume pricing

A team plan often monetizes a small number of high-value accounts more effectively than trying to extract more from every individual user.

## B. Usage-based pricing: targeted, transparent, and additive

Usage-based pricing should be used where:

1. The company incurs a meaningful variable cost, or  
2. The customer receives clearly measurable incremental value from additional usage.

Appropriate examples include:

- Processing credits
- High-volume generation
- Storage beyond a plan limit
- API calls
- Premium exports
- Advanced analysis
- High-speed or priority processing
- Additional team seats

Usage pricing should be an **add-on**, not a surprise penalty for normal use.

### Recommended structure

Each paid plan includes a generous allowance. Users can then:

- Purchase additional credits
- Upgrade to a higher tier
- Wait until the allowance resets
- Turn off or cap overage spending

The product should provide:

- A visible usage meter
- Forecasting of remaining capacity
- Warnings at approximately 70%, 85%, and 100%
- A hard spending cap by default
- One-tap purchase or upgrade
- Clear explanation of what consumed the allowance
- Refund or credit policy for accidental purchases

Do not interrupt a high-value workflow with an unexplained hard wall. At the point of limit, present three choices: wait, upgrade, or buy a clearly priced add-on.

## C. Advertising: narrow, native, and behaviorally controlled

Advertising should be treated as a supplemental revenue source, not the main answer to low subscription conversion. Since intrusive ads already harmed ratings, the company should apply strict constraints.

### Appropriate ad inventory

Prefer:

- Native placements in non-core screens
- Sponsored templates, content, tools, or recommendations
- Opt-in rewarded ads that unlock a discrete benefit
- Contextually relevant offers
- Ads shown primarily to low-intent or casual users
- Frequency-capped interstitials only at natural session breaks, if testing supports them

Avoid:

- Ads during core workflows
- Ads immediately after launch
- Full-screen ads after every action
- Ads that resemble system dialogs
- Ads that interrupt creation, saving, or sharing
- Targeting based on sensitive information
- Ads shown to paying users

### Recommended advertising treatment

- Casual explorers: limited native advertising or occasional sponsored content
- Habitual free users: primarily an upgrade proposition, with minimal ads
- High-intent users: no intrusive ads; use a clear ad-free Plus benefit
- Pro and Team users: no ads
- Dormant users: no increase in ad pressure; use reactivation messaging instead

An opt-in rewarded format can be especially useful if the user receives a meaningful benefit, such as one additional premium action, temporary capacity, or an export. The benefit must be explicit before the user watches the ad.

## D. Partnerships: monetize intent without degrading the product

Partnerships can monetize users who are valuable but unlikely to subscribe, especially when the app sits near a larger purchase or service decision.

Potential partnership models include:

- Affiliate referrals to complementary products
- Sponsored integrations
- Co-branded premium trials
- Bundling through telecom, device, financial, education, or productivity partners
- Revenue sharing for qualified leads
- Employer or institution-sponsored access
- Marketplace fees, where the app facilitates transactions
- White-label or embedded distribution

Partnerships should be relevant to the user’s active context. They should not turn the app into an advertising catalog.

Controls should include:

- Clear labeling of sponsored or affiliate content
- No sale of personal data without appropriate consent
- Frequency limits
- User controls and opt-outs
- Quality standards for partners
- Measurement of downstream complaints and trust
- No partner placement in moments where users are trying to complete a core task

Partnerships are most appropriate for casual users, dormant users, and users with specific commercial or professional intent. They should not substitute for a strong paid product.

---

# 4. Map offers to user segments

| Segment | Product treatment | Primary offer | Secondary monetization | Avoid |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Casual explorers | Preserve core use; lightweight onboarding; no early hard gate | Trial of Plus after demonstrated value | Native ads, relevant partnerships, opt-in rewards | Immediate paywall, frequent interstitials |
| Habitual free users | Show usage and time-saving benefits; personalize upgrade prompts | Plus monthly or annual plan | Limited ads, small paid add-ons | Generic upgrade banners on every screen |
| High-intent individual users | Identify premium behavior and present feature-specific value | Plus or Pro trial | Credits, premium add-ons | Charging before showing the benefit |
| Power users/prosumers | Show capacity, speed, quality, automation, and commercial value | Pro plan | Usage-based overage, API, commercial add-ons | Artificially low limits designed only to frustrate |
| Team/business users | Invite collaboration and central billing | Team/business plan | Seats, usage bundles, integrations | Forcing individual subscriptions for team behavior |
| Dormant users | Re-engage around prior value; reduce commercial pressure | Discounted annual plan or time-limited trial | Relevant partnership | More ads or immediate price increases |

## Trigger upgrade prompts based on “value moments”

Upgrade prompts should be tied to behavior such as:

- Completing a premium-adjacent workflow
- Reaching a meaningful usage threshold
- Attempting an advanced feature
- Returning repeatedly over a defined period
- Sharing or exporting frequently
- Inviting collaborators
- Experiencing a meaningful capacity or speed benefit

The prompt should answer:

1. What can the user do now?
2. What will improve after upgrading?
3. Why is the offer relevant to this action?
4. What does it cost?
5. Can the user cancel easily?

A user who has not yet activated should receive education and product guidance, not a subscription demand.

---

# 5. Packaging and pricing principles

## A. Use value fences, not arbitrary restrictions

A value fence separates paid and free users based on benefits that matter:

- More capacity
- Better quality
- Greater speed
- Advanced functionality
- Collaboration
- Commercial rights
- Convenience
- Support

An arbitrary restriction—such as blocking a basic action after a small number of uses—may increase short-term conversion but damage trust and retention.

## B. Test monthly and annual options

Offer:

- Monthly plan for low-commitment users
- Annual plan at a meaningful but controlled discount
- A short free trial for users who have already shown high intent
- No forced trial conversion without clear notice

The annual plan improves cash flow and retention but should not be used to conceal the product’s value or make cancellation difficult.

## C. Use regional and platform-aware pricing

Pricing should account for:

- Purchasing power
- Local competition
- App-store fees
- Tax treatment
- Payment methods
- Subscription norms
- Regulatory requirements

Do not test price only on the most engaged users. Price elasticity may differ materially by segment and geography.

## D. Consider a paid “event” or seasonal pass where usage is episodic

If the product is used heavily for occasional events, a one-time pass or monthly burst package may outperform a recurring subscription for some users. This can monetize episodic high-value use without forcing an annual commitment.

---

# 6. Experiment plan

The company should move from isolated feature tests to a controlled monetization program with persistent holdouts and explicit stopping rules.

## Phase 0: Instrumentation and baseline — weeks 1–4

Before changing paywalls or ads, establish:

- Segment definitions
- Current conversion funnel
- Activation rate
- Time to first value
- Feature-level usage
- Subscription trial start and conversion
- Refund and cancellation behavior
- Ad exposure and complaint rates
- App-store rating by acquisition cohort and geography
- Retention by segment and monetization treatment
- Revenue per MAU and revenue per retained user
- Variable cost per user

Create a permanent control group of approximately 5–10% of eligible users, depending on statistical power and business urgency. This group should remain on the existing experience for long-term comparison.

## Phase 1: Packaging tests — weeks 5–8

Test:

1. Free plus Plus versus free plus Plus and Pro
2. Feature-based value fences versus usage-based limits
3. Monthly-only versus monthly plus annual
4. Standard trial versus behavior-triggered trial
5. Ad-free as a Plus benefit versus additional premium features
6. Credit bundles versus automatic overage

Primary metrics:

- Upgrade-start rate
- Paid conversion at 7, 30, and 90 days
- Net revenue per user
- Trial-to-paid conversion
- Cancellation and refund rate
- Retention of new subscribers

Do not test multiple major pricing and paywall changes simultaneously in the same cohort unless the experiment is factorially designed.

## Phase 2: Offer and message personalization — weeks 9–12

For each segment, test:

- Feature-specific upgrade messages
- Capacity-based messaging
- Speed or quality messaging
- Annual-plan framing
- Personalized credit bundles
- Team invitation prompts
- Contextual partnership offers

Measure not only click-through but also **incremental revenue after churn and refunds**.

A message that produces more trial starts but also causes rapid cancellation may be worse than a lower-converting message.

## Phase 3: Advertising pilots — weeks 9–16

Test advertising only in small, randomized cohorts:

1. No ads
2. Native ads in low-friction surfaces
3. Opt-in rewarded ads
4. Limited session-break interstitials

Begin with casual and dormant users, not high-intent users.

Each ad test must include:

- Frequency caps
- A non-ad control
- App-store rating monitoring
- Complaint and support-ticket monitoring
- Uninstall monitoring
- Session-depth monitoring
- Revenue comparison over at least several weeks

The company should stop an ad treatment quickly if it increases ad revenue but reduces retained users enough to lower total LTV.

## Phase 4: Partnerships and team monetization — months 4–6

Pilot:

- One or two high-relevance affiliate partners
- One distribution or bundle partner
- Team workspaces for users showing collaboration behavior
- Sponsored premium trials
- Employer or institution-paid access where relevant

Partnership tests should be evaluated on net contribution, not gross referral revenue.

## Phase 5: Scale winners — months 6–12

Scale only treatments that:

- Increase net revenue per retained user
- Maintain acceptable retention
- Do not materially damage ratings
- Have manageable customer-support impact
- Comply with privacy and app-store requirements
- Are operationally and financially repeatable

---

# 7. Guardrail metrics and stopping rules

The prior failures show why monetization must be managed as a retention and trust problem, not only a revenue problem.

## A. Core business metrics

Track by segment, platform, geography, acquisition source, and treatment:

- Revenue per MAU
- Revenue per retained user
- Paid conversion at 7, 30, 90, and 180 days
- ARPPU
- Trial-to-paid conversion
- Monthly recurring revenue
- Annual-plan mix
- Net revenue after refunds, app-store fees, and incentives
- Customer acquisition payback
- LTV/CAC
- Variable cost to serve
- Gross margin by tier

## B. Retention and engagement guardrails

Track:

- D1, D7, D30, D90 retention
- Weekly and monthly active users
- Session frequency and duration
- Completion of the core action
- Activation rate
- Repeat use of the value-generating feature
- Churn and cancellation rate
- Reactivation rate
- Uninstall rate
- Downgrade rate
- Time to first value

### Illustrative stopping thresholds

The exact thresholds should be calibrated to historical volatility, but a treatment should generally be paused for investigation if it causes:

- More than **1 percentage point** deterioration in D30 retention
- More than **0.5 percentage points** deterioration in D7 retention for a high-volume cohort
- More than **10% relative increase** in uninstall rate
- More than **15% relative increase** in cancellation within the first billing cycle
- More than **20% relative increase** in refunds
- Material deterioration in completion of the core action
- A statistically significant decline in organic referrals or reactivation

For a change involving a hard paywall or advertising, use stricter thresholds because the downside can compound quickly.

## C. Trust and product-quality guardrails

Monitor daily during launches:

- App-store rating
- One-star review rate
- Reviews mentioning ads, paywalls, price, or cancellation
- Support tickets per 1,000 users
- Payment failures
- Accidental purchase complaints
- Privacy or consent complaints
- Ad hide/report rates
- Latency and crash rates
- Feature-access confusion
- Cancellation friction

A rating decline of even a few tenths can materially affect organic acquisition. The team should compare rating trends against the control group and against seasonality, not rely only on aggregate rating.

## D. Segment-level protections

A positive aggregate result can conceal damage to an important segment. Require separate reporting for:

- New users
- Existing active users
- High-value users
- Users on older devices
- Users in lower-income regions
- Users acquired organically
- Users with accessibility needs
- Users with high support or cost-to-serve profiles

---

# 8. Experiment governance

Every monetization experiment should have a one-page approval document containing:

- Hypothesis
- Target segment
- Eligibility criteria
- Control treatment
- Treatment details
- Price and offer
- Expected revenue effect
- Expected retention risk
- Primary metric
- Guardrail metrics
- Minimum sample and duration
- Stop conditions
- Rollback owner
- Privacy and app-store review
- Post-test decision date

## Use staged exposure

For any material paywall, pricing, or ad change:

1. Internal test
2. 1% of eligible users
3. 5%
4. 10–25%
5. Broad rollout only after guardrails remain healthy

Monitor new treatments daily during the first week and at least weekly through the first billing cycle. Subscription and retention tests should not be judged only on short-term click-through.

## Maintain long-term holdouts

Keep a small holdout group for each major monetization strategy. This identifies:

- Delayed churn
- Organic acquisition changes
- Long-term rating effects
- Whether revenue is incremental or merely accelerated
- Whether users adapt to or become fatigued by an offer

---

# 9. Operating cadence and accountability

Create a Monetization Council led by the Chief Product Officer or Chief Growth Officer, with Finance, Data, Marketing, Engineering, Customer Support, Legal, and Trust/Safety representation.

The council should review weekly:

- Experiment performance
- Revenue and retention tradeoffs
- Rating and complaint trends
- Segment migration
- Subscription cancellations
- Ad load and yield
- Partner quality
- Rollbacks and next decisions

Each monetization stream should have one accountable owner:

| Stream | Accountable owner |
|---|---|
| Subscription packaging | Product/Growth |
| Pricing and revenue model | Finance plus Growth |
| Usage metering and credits | Product/Engineering |
| Advertising quality and yield | Monetization/Ads |
| Partnerships | Business Development |
| Retention and customer experience | Lifecycle/Customer Success |
| Guardrails and causal measurement | Data Science |
| Privacy and app-store compliance | Legal/Trust |

Variable compensation should reward **net revenue growth with retention and rating safeguards**, not conversion or ad impressions alone.

---

# 10. Recommended first 90 days

## Days 1–15: establish the facts

- Define behavioral segments.
- Build the revenue-per-MAU baseline.
- Identify premium-adjacent actions and variable-cost drivers.
- Freeze further aggressive paywall and ad expansion.
- Establish control groups and dashboards.
- Audit current cancellation, refund, rating, and complaint data.

## Days 16–30: design the offer architecture

- Finalize Free, Plus, and Pro packaging.
- Define whether usage-based credits are economically justified.
- Specify team/business signals and initial offer.
- Design a low-ad-load treatment for casual users only.
- Select one or two partnership categories.
- Establish price and regional test cells.

## Days 31–60: run low-risk tests

- Launch behavior-triggered Plus trials.
- Test feature-based versus capacity-based fences.
- Test monthly and annual packaging.
- Pilot credits with clear caps and warnings.
- Test native or rewarded ads with casual users.
- Monitor retention, uninstall, reviews, and support daily.

## Days 61–90: make evidence-based decisions

- Roll back treatments that fail guardrails.
- Scale winning subscription offers.
- Introduce Pro or team prompts to qualified users.
- Expand only the ad format that preserves retention and ratings.
- Launch the first relevant partnership pilot.
- Recalculate the 12-month revenue forecast using observed net economics.

---

# 11. Definition of success

By day 30:

- Users are behaviorally segmented.
- The company has a clear Free, Plus, and Pro architecture.
- Monetization dashboards and control groups are operating.
- No new high-risk paywall or ad treatment is launched without guardrails.

By day 90:

- Behavior-triggered offers have improved paid conversion or revenue per retained user.
- Subscription trials are converting without a material increase in early cancellation.
- Usage-based pricing is working as an optional add-on for high-value users.
- Advertising is limited to formats and segments that do not damage ratings or retention.
- The company has evidence on at least one viable partnership channel.

By month 12:

- Paid conversion has increased materially without recreating the prior uninstall spike.
- ARPPU and blended revenue per MAU have improved.
- Revenue is diversified across subscriptions, selective usage revenue, and relevant partnerships.
- Free users still receive a credible core product.
- App-store ratings, D30/D90 retention, and organic acquisition remain within approved tolerance.

The central principle is to monetize **the incremental value users recognize**, not merely to restrict access. High-intent users should receive compelling paid outcomes, casual users should be monetized lightly, and every material monetization change should be judged on retained net revenue rather than immediate conversion alone.

The output is comprehensive and directionally sound, but it remains too generic to serve as an execution-ready monetization strategy.

### Key weaknesses

- **No product-specific economics or pricing.** It recommends Free, Plus, Pro, credits, ads, and partnerships without specifying price points, expected mix, margin, or revenue contribution. The proposed 4–6% conversion and 15–30% ARPPU increase are labeled “plausible” but are not supported by a model. - **The user segments are hypothetical.** The response says usage data shows distinct segments, but it invents generic segments rather than explaining how to derive them from the company’s actual data. One accountable owner should decide pricing, with Finance, Product, Data, Legal, and Support as required inputs. The response would also benefit from a clear approval process for experiments that can affect app-store reputation.

The strategy should begin with a quantified baseline by segment, then select one primary monetization path based on value and unit economics. It should provide:

The company should pursue a **subscription-led, segment-specific monetization model**:

- **80% of monetization effort:** improve subscription conversion and packaging.

| Segment | Definition from observed behavior | % of MAU | D30 retention | Current paid rate | Current revenue/user | Cost to serve | Likely willingness to pay |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Segment A: low-intent/casual | Low frequency and shallow use | Actual data | Actual data | Actual data | Actual data | Actual data | Low |

## How to derive the segments

Illustrative starting thresholds might be:

- **Low-intent:** fewer than 3 active days per month and no premium-adjacent action.
- **Habitual:** 3–14 active days per month with repeated core use.
- **High-intent:** at least two premium-feature attempts or three visits to a premium-adjacent workflow in 30 days.
- **Power:** top 10% of usage volume or users whose variable cost is materially above the median.
- **Collaborative/commercial:** at least two invitations, shares, exports, or workspace behaviors in 30 days.
- **Dormant:** previously active for at least three months, then no meaningful activity for 30 days.

These are starting rules only. A segment is valid if it has:

- At least 5% of MAU or a strategically material revenue contribution
- Statistically different retention, usage, or willingness-to-pay behavior
- A distinct monetization treatment that can be explained to users
- Stable membership over time
- Predictive power for conversion or LTV in an out-of-sample test

The baseline should also report **segment migration**. A user should move from “habitual” to “high-intent” when behavior changes; the company should not continue showing the same offer indefinitely.

---

# 2. Economic objective and 12-month revenue model

## Target metrics

The company should set a 12-month target based on actual baseline revenue, but a reasonable planning objective is:

- Increase **net revenue per MAU by at least 2.0x**
- Increase **contribution margin per retained user by at least 50%**
- Keep D30 retention within **0.5 percentage points** of control
- Keep D90 retention within **1 percentage point** of control
- Keep the app-store rating within **0.1 stars** of the pre-test baseline
- Achieve at least **70% first-renewal rate** for new monthly subscribers, unless the category baseline is materially different
- Reach paid conversion only if the resulting subscribers remain profitable after refunds, app-store fees, support, and variable costs

## Illustrative scenario model

The following example assumes:

- 1 million MAU
- Current paid conversion of 1.8%
- Current net paid ARPPU of $8 per month after app-store fees, refunds, and discounts
- Current non-subscription revenue of $0.03 per MAU per month

Current monthly net revenue per MAU is approximately:

\[
(1.8\% \times \$8.00) + \$0.03 = \$0.174
\]

The scenarios below show the required economics, not a forecast.

| Metric | Conservative | Base | Upside |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Paid conversion | 3.0% | 4.0% | 5.0% |
| Net paid ARPPU/month | $8.50 | $9.50 | $10.50 |
| Subscription revenue/MAU | $0.255 | $0.380 | $0.525 |
| Usage-add-on revenue/MAU | $0.020 | $0.050 | $0.080 |
| Ad revenue/MAU | $0.035 | $0.050 | $0.070 |
| Partnership revenue/MAU | $0.005 | $0.020 | $0.035 |
| **Total net revenue/MAU** | **$0.315** | **$0.500** | **$0.710** |
| Increase versus $0.174 baseline | 81% | 187% | 308% |
| Contribution margin target | 55%+ | 60%+ | 62%+ |

For 1 million MAU, the base case represents approximately **$500,000 in monthly net revenue**, compared with approximately $174,000 under the assumed baseline.

The base case should be rejected if achieving 4% paid conversion requires materially worse D30 retention, higher refunds, or increased support costs. In that event, the company should prefer a lower conversion rate with higher retention and ARPPU.

## Revenue bridge and ownership

| Revenue stream | Base-case share of incremental revenue | Accountable owner | Initial priority |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Subscription packaging and conversion | 65–75% | Chief Product/Growth Officer | Highest |
| Paid usage add-ons | 15–20% | Product monetization lead | Second |
| Advertising | 5–10% | Ads/monetization lead | Controlled test only |
| Partnerships | 5–10% | Partnerships lead | Only where intent is proven |

One person—the **Chief Product/Growth Officer**—should be accountable for the complete monetization P&L and final product decision. Finance, Data, Legal, Engineering, Support, and Trust/Safety provide required input but do not share final accountability.

---

# 3. Recommended offer architecture

The product should use a four-level architecture only if the data supports distinct value fences.

## Free: preserve the habit and the core outcome

Free users should retain:

- The primary use case
- The core “aha” moment
- Basic creation or consumption
- Basic saving or sharing
- Enough monthly use to form a habit
- Access to the product’s fundamental output

Do not place these behind a paywall:

- First-use activation
- Completion of a basic core task
- Access to previously created user content
- Essential sharing or export required for normal use
- A workflow already started by the user

## Plus: sell a better everyday experience

Illustrative starting price:

- **$7.99/month**
- **$59.99/year**—approximately 37% below twelve monthly payments

Potential fences:

- Ad-free use
- Higher but predictable usage allowance
- Longer history or storage
- Faster processing
- Better customization
- Cross-device continuity
- Basic premium features
- Priority support

The Plus tier should be targeted primarily at habitual free users who have already demonstrated recurring value.

## Pro: sell a superior outcome

Illustrative starting price:

- **$14.99/month**
- **$119.99/year**

Potential fences:

- Advanced automation
- Highest quality or resolution
- Batch processing
- Priority capacity
- Advanced analytics
- Commercial-use rights
- Large storage or history
- Integrations or API access
- Higher included usage allowance

Pro must offer a meaningfully different outcome, not merely a slightly higher limit.

## Team or business

Launch only after observing enough collaborative or commercial behavior to justify it.

Illustrative starting prices:

- **$12–$18 per seat/month**
- Minimum three seats
- Optional usage bundle priced separately

Potential fences:

- Shared workspaces
- Central billing
- Admin controls
- Usage reporting
- Shared templates or assets
- Permissioning
- Business support
- Security or compliance features

A team plan should be offered when a user invites collaborators, repeatedly shares work, or uses the product in a commercial workflow—not shown indiscriminately to all users.

## Episodic pass

If the product has seasonal or event-driven usage, test a one-time package:

- **$4.99–$9.99 for a defined period or usage bundle**

This is appropriate for users with high short-term value but low willingness to maintain a recurring subscription.

---

# 4. Precise value fences

The company should classify every feature into one of four groups:

| Feature class | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Core activation and basic outcome | Free |
| Repeated convenience improvement | Plus |
| Superior quality, speed, automation, or commercial outcome | Pro |
| Incremental capacity with measurable cost/value | Optional usage purchase |

Examples of defensible paid fences include:

- More capacity after the user has successfully used the free allowance
- Faster processing when speed has observable value
- Higher output quality
- Batch or automated workflows
- Advanced personalization
- Commercial rights
- Team administration
- Extended history or storage
- Premium integrations

Avoid arbitrary fences such as blocking a basic action after one or two uses. The user should understand exactly what they are buying and why it matters.

Upgrade prompts should occur after:

- A completed value moment
- A repeated premium-feature attempt
- A meaningful usage threshold
- A collaboration signal
- A high-frequency return pattern
- A clear capacity or speed need

The prompt should show the feature or outcome first, explain the incremental benefit, display the full price, and make cancellation terms visible.

---

# 5. Usage-based pricing with strong trust protections

Usage pricing should be an optional supplement, not an involuntary overage system.

## Recommended policy

- Every paid tier includes a generous allowance.
- **Overages are opt-in only.**
- Users cannot be charged automatically beyond their plan without explicit consent.
- Default spending cap is $0.
- Users see a meter and projected depletion date.
- Warnings occur at 70%, 85%, and 100%.
- Credits are clearly tied to a unit users understand.
- Unused paid credits roll over for at least three months; included credits may expire at renewal if clearly disclosed.
- Refunds or credit reversals apply to accidental purchases and failed processing.
- A task already in progress is completed under the user’s existing allowance; the app must not interrupt or discard work mid-flow.
- At the limit, users can wait, upgrade, or buy a clearly priced bundle.
- The user can disable usage purchases in settings.

Test bundles such as:

- 50 units for $4.99
- 150 units for $9.99
- 500 units for $24.99

These prices must be tied to the product’s actual unit cost and user-perceived value. A bundle should target at least **70% gross margin** unless the usage is strategically important for acquisition or conversion.

---

# 6. Advertising: default to no interstitials

Given the previous rating damage, the default policy should be:

- No launch-screen ads
- No ads during core tasks
- No ads immediately before saving, sharing, or exporting
- No ads for paying users
- No full-screen interstitials unless a separate experiment demonstrates clear net benefit
- No ads targeted using sensitive personal information

## Initial advertising tests

Only test with low-intent, non-paying users:

1. No ads
2. One native placement in a non-core screen
3. One opt-in rewarded ad that unlocks a defined benefit

Rewarded benefits might include:

- One additional premium action
- Temporary capacity
- A limited export
- A short-term enhancement

The user must know the benefit before opting in.

The company should use a reputable mediation stack, block unsafe categories, review creative quality, and maintain a partner blocklist. Ad tests should be evaluated on **net retained revenue**, not eCPM alone.

Ads should be removed from a treatment if they cause:

- A confidence-adjusted D30 retention decline above the approved limit
- A material increase in uninstalls
- A rating decline beyond the launch gate
- A decline in organic acquisition
- Increased complaints or support contacts
- Lower completion of the core action

Interstitials should not be part of the first 90-day plan.

---

# 7. Partnerships: gated, contextual, and economically justified

Partnerships should not be a general-purpose revenue strategy. Test them only where the app reveals a specific user intent.

Prioritize one of the following based on observed behavior:

- A complementary tool frequently used after the app
- A relevant professional service
- Employer- or institution-sponsored access
- A device, telecom, or platform bundle that can reduce acquisition cost
- A highly relevant affiliate offer shown after a commercial-intent action

Approve a partnership only if it meets all of these requirements:

- User intent is observable without relying on sensitive data.
- Expected net revenue per exposed user is at least **2x incremental support and integration cost**.
- The partner passes brand-safety, privacy, and quality review.
- The offer is clearly labeled as sponsored or affiliate content.
- The user can dismiss or opt out.
- It does not interrupt a core workflow.
- Attribution can distinguish incremental revenue from users who would have purchased anyway.

Do not pursue marketplace, employer, or complex integration models in the first 90 days unless the app already has proven commercial or collaborative usage.

---

# 8. Segment-specific monetization plan

| Segment | Entry criteria | Primary offer | Secondary offer | Treatment to avoid |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low-intent/casual | Low frequency, no premium behavior | Free product | Native or rewarded ads; contextual partner offer | Early paywall or interstitials |
| Habitual free | Repeated core use, no premium conversion | Plus at $7.99/month or annual plan | Ad-free upgrade, small credit bundle | Generic prompts every session |
| High-intent individual | Repeated premium attempts or high-value outcomes | Behavior-triggered Plus/Pro trial | Feature add-on or annual plan | Blocking the first premium experience |
| Power/high-volume | Top usage decile or high variable cost | Pro at $14.99/month | Opt-in credits or higher tier | Artificially low free limits |
| Collaborative/commercial | Invites, sharing, exports, work use | Team plan or commercial rights | Seats, integrations, usage bundles | Individual-only pricing |
| Dormant | Formerly active, now inactive | Reactivation trial or episodic pass | Relevant partnership | Increased ad load or aggressive paywall |

Each offer should be personalized to the user’s actual behavior. For example:

- “You used [feature] three times this week. Plus includes unlimited access and removes ads.”
- “You are approaching your monthly processing limit. Upgrade for 200 included actions or buy a one-time bundle.”
- “Invite two collaborators to create a shared workspace.”

---

# 9. Pricing, trials, and billing policies

## Price experiments

Test a limited, explicit price ladder:

- Plus: $5.99, $7.99, $9.99 per month
- Pro: $11.99, $14.99, $19.99 per month
- Annual plans at 25–40% below monthlyized pricing
- One-time pass at $4.99–$9.99 where episodic use exists

Randomize price only within the same geography, platform, and eligibility group. Do not expose adjacent users to different prices in a way that creates sharing or trust problems.

## Regional pricing

Use purchasing-power-adjusted prices, local currencies, taxes, and payment methods. Analyze price elasticity by:

- Country
- Platform
- Acquisition source
- Segment
- New versus existing user

## Trials and introductory offers

- Show a trial only after meaningful product use or premium intent.
- Use a clear end date and renewal price.
- Send reminders before conversion.
- Make cancellation as easy as purchase.
- Test a 7-day trial against a 14-day trial only with sufficient post-trial observation.
- Test a first-month discount separately from a free trial; do not combine both initially.
- Limit repeated trial eligibility to prevent abuse.

## Existing subscribers

- Grandfather existing subscribers for at least one billing cycle when changing packaging.
- Give advance notice of price increases.
- Offer an equivalent or better entitlement when migrating plans.
- Do not remove a previously paid-for feature without a clear remedy.
- Test annual-plan migration only after measuring renewal and support impact.

All billing, disclosure, refund, and cancellation flows must comply with app-store rules and local subscription law.

---

# 10. Experiment program

## Phase 0: instrumentation and baseline — weeks 1–3

Implement event-level measurement for:

- Activation and first value
- Core-task completion
- Premium-feature attempts
- Usage and cost units
- Paywall impressions
- Trial starts
- Subscription purchases
- Renewal, cancellation, downgrade, refund, and chargeback
- Ad impressions, dismissals, reports, and revenue
- Partner clicks and downstream revenue
- Ratings, review sentiment, support contacts, and uninstalls
- Organic installs and referral activity

Create a persistent **business holdout of 2–3% of eligible users**, not automatically 5–10%. The size must be based on power and revenue cost. Use separate short-term controls for individual experiments.

## Experiment 1: value-triggered subscription offer — weeks 4–8

**Hypothesis:** A prompt shown after repeated premium intent will increase paid conversion without harming retention compared with a generic paywall.

- Randomization unit: user account
- Stratification: segment, geography, platform, acquisition source
- Control: current monetization experience
- Treatment: behavior-triggered Plus or Pro offer
- Primary metric: 30-day incremental net revenue per eligible user
- Secondary metrics: paid conversion, first renewal, refund rate
- Duration: at least 30 days, with renewal observed through 60–90 days

## Experiment 2: packaging and price — weeks 5–10

Test:

- Plus only versus Plus + Pro
- $5.99 versus $7.99 versus $9.99
- Monthly versus monthly plus annual
- Feature fence versus capacity fence

Do not test price, paywall design, and feature entitlements simultaneously unless using a planned factorial design.

## Experiment 3: optional usage bundles — weeks 7–12

Test:

- No bundle
- 50 units for $4.99
- 150 units for $9.99

Use only high-intent and power users. Measure net contribution after variable cost, refund rate, and whether bundles reduce subscription upgrades.

## Experiment 4: native and rewarded ads — weeks 8–14

Use casual users only:

- No ads
- One native placement
- One rewarded placement

No interstitials in the initial test. Continue measurement for at least 30 days after exposure begins.

## Experiment 5: contextual partnership — months 3–5

Test one partner offer against no offer among users showing a defined commercial-intent signal. Evaluate net incremental contribution, not click-through rate.

---

# 11. Statistical design and decision rules

## Sample size

The Data Science lead should calculate sample size before launch using baseline rates, minimum detectable effects, power, and expected traffic.

As an initial reference:

- Detecting a rise in paid conversion from 2.0% to 2.6% at 80% power and 95% confidence generally requires approximately **10,000–15,000 users per arm**, depending on allocation and baseline variance.
- Detecting a 1 percentage-point change in D30 retention may require substantially more users; if traffic is insufficient, use a sequential Bayesian or variance-reduction design rather than pretending the test is conclusive.
- Revenue tests should be powered on user-level revenue, typically requiring longer duration because revenue is skewed and delayed.

Use:

- User-level randomization
- Stratified assignment
- Intention-to-treat analysis
- Pre-registered primary metrics
- CUPED or equivalent variance reduction where available
- Sequential testing boundaries for interim reads
- False-discovery-rate control when running multiple related variants

Do not repeatedly inspect noisy results and declare a winner without a pre-approved stopping rule.

## Minimum observation windows

| Test type | Minimum read window |
|---|---|
| Paywall click or trial start | 7 days |
| Purchase conversion | 30 days |
| Monthly subscription renewal | 60–90 days |
| Annual subscription value | At least 90 days for early indicators; 12 months for final LTV |
| Ads | 30 days, including uninstall and rating effects |
| D30 retention | 30 days after the final eligible user enters |
| Referral/organic effects | 60–90 days |

---

# 12. Guardrails and hard launch gates

Every experiment must have a primary metric, economic threshold, and pre-approved rollback owner.

## Hard launch gates

A treatment cannot scale beyond 25% of eligible users if, versus control, it shows any of the following with a 95% confidence interval excluding the approved tolerance:

- D30 retention decline greater than **0.5 percentage points**
- D90 retention decline greater than **1.0 percentage point**
- Core-task completion decline greater than **0.5 percentage points**
- Uninstall increase greater than **5% relative**
- First-cycle cancellation increase greater than **10% relative**
- Refund or chargeback increase greater than **15% relative**
- App-store rating decline greater than **0.1 stars** over a minimum of 5,000 exposed users
- Rating-adjusted negative sentiment increase greater than **10% relative**
- Organic installs or referrals decline greater than **5% relative** after at least 30 days
- Support contacts increase greater than **10% per 1,000 exposed users**
- Contribution margin per retained user declines

A statistically significant result that is commercially immaterial should not automatically trigger a rollback. Conversely, a severe trust or product-quality failure should trigger a pause immediately, even before statistical certainty is reached.

## Immediate rollback triggers

Pause within 24 hours for:

- Incorrect billing or duplicate charges
- Inability to cancel
- Privacy or consent failure
- Core workflows blocked unexpectedly
- Material increase in crashes or latency
- Unsafe or misleading advertising
- One-star review spike linked to the treatment
- Users losing access to paid-for content or work

---

# 13. Subscription health and long-term economics

A subscription winner must pass all of these tests:

\[
\text{12-month contribution LTV}
>
\text{Customer acquisition cost}
+
\text{discounts}
+
\text{support}
+
\text{payment/refund costs}
\]

Track by cohort:

- Trial-to-paid conversion
- First renewal at month one
- Second renewal at month two or three
- Monthly gross churn
- Annual renewal
- Downgrades
- Refunds and chargebacks
- Net revenue after platform fees
- Support cost
- Usage cost
- Organic referrals
- Acquisition volume after launch

A treatment that increases first-month purchases but lowers second-renewal rates should not be scaled. The primary subscription decision metric should be **90-day net contribution per eligible user**, with 12-month LTV as the ultimate validation metric.

---

# 14. Rollout and rollback plan

For every material change:

1. Internal dogfood and billing validation
2. 1% of eligible users for 48–72 hours
3. 5% for one week
4. 10–25% through the first meaningful retention checkpoint
5. Broad rollout only after economic and guardrail criteria pass

The rollout owner maintains:

- Versioned treatment configuration
- Eligibility rules
- Exposure logs
- Kill switch
- Customer-support script
- Refund and remediation process
- Daily rating and complaint review
- Formal post-test decision

If a treatment fails, restore the prior experience immediately, contact affected users where billing or access was involved, issue credits or refunds as appropriate, and document the failure before retesting.

---

# 15. First 90 days

## Days 1–14: establish facts

- Build the segment and cohort baseline.
- Calculate current net revenue and contribution margin per MAU.
- Identify premium-adjacent actions and variable-cost drivers.
- Freeze expansion of aggressive paywalls and intrusive ads.
- Instrument billing, retention, rating, and organic-acquisition metrics.
- Assign one monetization P&L owner.
- Define experiment approval and rollback procedures.

## Days 15–30: finalize the offer

- Confirm Free, Plus, and Pro entitlements.
- Select initial prices and regional test cells.
- Define the precise free-tier value fences.
- Design opt-in usage bundles.
- Define trial, renewal, cancellation, refund, and grandfathering policies.
- Select one partnership hypothesis based on actual user intent.
- Establish the business holdout and test-specific controls.

## Days 31–60: run low-risk tests

- Launch behavior-triggered Plus offers.
- Test packaging and prices.
- Test annual versus monthly presentation.
- Pilot optional usage bundles with power users.
- Test one native and one rewarded ad format with casual users.
- Monitor retention, reviews, support, and uninstall data daily.

## Days 61–90: decide and scale selectively

- Scale only treatments that improve 30-day net contribution without breaching gates.
- Continue subscription cohorts through first renewal.
- Roll back any treatment that damages core-task completion, trust, or ratings.
- Introduce Pro or Team prompts only to qualified users.
- Launch one contextual partnership pilot if economics are proven.
- Reforecast the 12-month plan using observed segment sizes, conversion, churn, ARPPU, ad yield, and cost to serve.

---

# Definition of success

By day 30:

- Every material user segment has a measured size, retention profile, cost-to-serve estimate, and monetization hypothesis.
- The company has a quantified revenue baseline and price-test plan.
- Free-tier fences are explicitly defined.
- Experiment controls, guardrails, and rollback mechanisms are operating.

By day 90:

- A behavior-triggered subscription offer has been tested through a meaningful retention window.
- Pricing and packaging decisions are based on net contribution, not trial starts alone.
- Optional usage bundles have been tested without surprise overages or interrupted workflows.
- Advertising is limited to native or rewarded formats that pass retention and rating gates.
- At least one partnership has been evaluated on incremental economics.

By month 12:

- Net revenue per MAU has increased by at least 2x in the base case, while contribution margin per retained user improves.
- Subscription growth comes primarily from high-intent and habitual users rather than forced conversion.
- Usage revenue is additive and opt-in.
- Advertising remains limited to users and contexts where it does not damage trust.
- Renewals, ratings, organic acquisition, and D30/D90 retention remain within approved tolerances.

The strategic principle is simple: **keep the core free, charge for recognized incremental value, make variable usage transparent and voluntary, and scale only monetization that produces more retained contribution than it destroys in churn and trust.**
